21705-in-the-track-of-the-troops:
War in Europe gives R. M. Ballantyne the setting for this tale of a young man swept along behind an army. The narrator tells his own story, starting with his boyhood love of taking things apart to see how they worked. That habit of pulling the world to pieces shapes the teller of the tale. He writes with pride, humor, and a strong wish to seem wise.

What follows is a string of personal adventures in the path of marching troops. Ballantyne mixes real scenes of modern war with the narrator's mishaps and narrow escapes. The result is part war report and part comic confession, told in a voice that keeps undercutting its own grand claims.
21749-man-on-the-ocean-a-book-about-boat:
Ships themselves are the subject of this Ballantyne book, which calls a great ship one of the most wonderful things men have made. A ship, he says, is a wooden house built to float, a small moving hotel on the sea. It carries its own little country of people across trackless water for months at a time.

The chapters walk through boats and ships of many kinds and ages. Ballantyne explains how they are built, rigged, sailed, and handled in storms. He wrote it for readers who loved his sea tales and wanted the facts behind them. It is a plain-spoken tour of man's oldest great machine, told by a man who never tired of the sea.
21976-three-years-in-the-sixth-corps:
The Sixth Corps of the Army of the Potomac gets its chronicle in George T. Stevens's Three Years in the Sixth Corps, published at Albany in 1866. Stevens served as surgeon of the 77th New York Volunteers. He offers the book to his old comrades, hoping it recalls their varied experiences in an unparalleled body of men. General John Sedgwick, the corps' beloved commander, fronts the volume.

Stevens wrote mostly from notes taken amid the scenes themselves, with official reports and officers' letters in support. Marches, battles, camps, and hospital scenes pass in order from 1861 to April 1865. He promises no exaggeration and asks brave men's leniency for faults. As a unit history by a man who marched with it, the book keeps a surgeon's eye and a soldier's loyalty.
2689-over-the-teacups:
Oliver W. Holmes wrote this late series of papers over the teacups, pleased by a kind reception greater than he had dared to hope. A late comer among ardent candidates for public attention, he feared he had already had his day, like the Frenchman told he had come again.

The papers that follow chat about age, books, science, and Boston life, with the Doctor's familiar wit. Holmes writes as an old friend at the table, not a lecturer. The book charms as a farewell performance, gentle, learned, and full of the humor of a long life.
3462-more-hunting-wasps:
Jean Henri Fabre completes his wasp essays in this volume, the third part of his collected work on wasps after The Hunting Wasps and the Mason Wasps. Fourteen chapters cover the Ammophila, the Bembex, and other hunting wasps, following how each kind captures prey, digs a nest, and stocks it for its young. Notes point readers back to earlier chapters for fuller accounts.

Fabre's method is patient watching in the field, not laboratory theory. He records the wasp's sting, its choice of caterpillar, and its care for eggs it will never see hatch. The book suits readers who enjoy natural history written with clarity and wonder, and it closes a set that made Fabre famous among insect lovers.
4540-in-his-steps:
Charles M. Sheldon sets this Christian novel in an American town church, opening with the Reverend Henry Maxwell struggling to finish his Sunday sermon. Maxwell, his wife Mary, and their congregation are soon faced with a simple, hard question drawn from the Bible: what would Jesus do in their place? The story asks its readers to take that question out of church and into daily work.

Members of the church pledge to act on the question for a year, and their choices touch business, newspapers, charity, art, and family life. Some lose money or standing, while others find a new purpose. Sheldon writes plainly, aiming at conscience rather than fine style. Readers get a moral tale that has shaped church discussion for generations, and a clear picture of its famous challenge in action.
558-the-thirty-nine-steps:
John Buchan launches Richard Hannay in this brisk spy tale, written during an illness in 1915. Hannay, bored after three months in London, takes in a stranger who dies that night, leaving a notebook of a German plot. Fleeing police and spies, Hannay runs across Scotland by train, road, and moor.

Buchan writes in lean, fast prose, praising the shocker where events march just inside the possible. A literary innkeeper, a radical candidate, and a dry-fly fisherman mark the chase. The novel endures as the model modern thriller, where one man must stop a war plot with wit alone.
8801-drum-taps:
Walt Whitman gathers his Civil War poems in Drum-Taps, opening with songs for a prelude, eighteen sixty-one, and the famous call, beat, beat, drums. From Paumanok starting I fly like a bird, Song of the Banner at Daybreak. Rise O Days from your fathomless deeps, Virginia the West, City of Ships, and The Centenarian's Story follow. Cavalry crossing a ford, bivouac on a mountainside, an army corps on the march, and by the bivouac's fitful flame bring the war's camps and marches close.

Come up from the fields father, Vigil strange I kept on the field one night, A march in the ranks hard-pressed. The Wound-Dresser show Whitman's other war: nursing, mourning, and endurance. The poems were written as the war happened, by a poet who visited hospitals and knew its cost.
9490-quaint-courtships:
Quaint Courtships, a Harper's collection from 1906, gathers short love tales by a roster of noted American writers. William Dean Howells and Henry Mills Alden edited the set. Names inside include Margaret Deland, Mary E. Wilkins Freeman, and Norman Duncan. Each tale turns on courtship, in its odd, shy, or comic forms.

Deland opens with an encore tale of Old Chester, where a staid captain of seventy finds romance late in life. Other tales move from a harbor town to city rooms, each with its own wooing snag. The tone stays light and fond, with old-style manners throughout. A reader gets a charming sampler of early 1900s American short fiction, all on love's crooked path.
9873-till-the-clock-stops:
J. J. Bell's 1917 novel opens in a London City boardroom, where a young man signs a plain-looking deed for the Aasvogel Syndicate. The deed is filed away and forgotten, but in due season it bears a weighty crop of complex and extraordinary consequences.

Bell, known for his Scottish humor in Wee Macgreegor, here turns to a London tale of business, chance, and fate. The story follows how one quiet act ripples outward into trouble and surprise for everyone touched by it. Readers get a well-made popular novel about small causes and large results.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adolphe-decha:
Adolphe Dechamps, Belgian statesman and publicist and brother of Cardinal Dechamps, was born at Melle near Ghent on 17 June 1807 and died at Manage on 19 July 1875. His public life began about 1830, soon growing popular through brilliant contributions to Catholic newspapers. With his friend de Decker he founded La Revue de Bruxelles, advocating a system called government of the centres.

Under that scheme, ministries would mix Catholics and Liberals, backed by the moderate elements of both parties. The plan worked successfully for some years, though Dechamps saw that Catholics and Liberals must sooner or later part unless Catholics surrendered their principles. Elected to the Chamber of Representatives in 1834, he won prominence as orator and practical statesman. He debated communal organization in 1836, opposed the Dutch treaty in 1839, and wrote on parties, schools, and Bismarck.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-ear:
Six bishops named Alexander are sketched. Alexander of Antioch, thirty-eighth bishop of that see from 413 to 421, earns Theodoret's praise for a holy and austere life. Alexander of Apamea, a Syrian bishop at Ephesus in 431, numbered among eight bishops John's party sent to Emperor Theodosius. Alexander of Basilinopolis in Bithynia, St. John Chrysostom's friend, owed his see to the saint and retired about 410 after his patron's fall.

Alexander of Byzantium, as Constantinople was then called, took his see at seventy-three during the first Arian troubles. Alexander of Hierapolis stood unbending against St. Cyril at Ephesus and for Nestorius, even when others yielded. Alexander of Jerusalem, friend of Origen and fellow student under Pantaenus and Clement at Alexandria, became bishop of a see in Cappadocia or Cilicia. The six sketches show how widely the name runs through the early Church's disputes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-steps:
Altars at first stood without steps, catacomb altars on the pavement and church altars over the confession, where martyrs' remains lay. By the fourth century the altar stood one step above the sanctuary floor. Today the high altar's steps number unevenly for symbolical reasons, usually three, five, or seven including the predella, passing around three sides.

Wood, stone, or brick may form them, though St. Charles wanted the lower two or four of stone or brick and the wooden predella for the celebrant. Each step runs about a foot broad and six inches high, the predella about three feet six inches broad in front and one foot at the sides. Side altars need at least one step.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-early-christi:
Early Christian lamps are small clay lamps marked with Christian symbols, among the commonest relics of Christian antiquity. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that they turn up in all ancient Christian centers, but the Roman catacombs hold them in striking numbers, many without any clear Christian mark. They fall into two groups, the older make of the early imperial age and the type of the Constantinian age.

This modest craft itself declined from the first century to the fourth or fifth, and earlier lamps show far finer workmanship. Forms differ too, and the entry points to Smith and Cheetham, Lowrie, and Leclercq for the details. A little lamp thus becomes a witness to taste, trade, and faith in the ancient Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-etienne-agard:
Etienne Agard de Champs, a distinguished theologian and author, was born at Bourges on 2 September 1613. He died at Paris on 31 July 1701, though De Backer gives La Fleche. He joined the Jesuit noviciate in 1630, and in Paris he later taught rhetoric, philosophy, and theology. Rector at Rennes and three times at Paris, he also headed the professed house and served twice as provincial of France and once as provincial of Lyons.

Jansenism, the great debate of France in his day, fills all his books. Under the name Richard Antonius he wrote the Defensio Censurae Sacrae Facultatis Parisiensis. Well received, it passed through five editions in two years. Vincent Lenis answered in his Theriaca of 1648, prompting Champs's Responsio ad objectiones Vincentianas of 1648. He defended the Sorbonne in De Haeresi Janseniana of 1654. His best known other work is Le secret du Jansenisme découvert et refute par un Docteur Catholique of 1651.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eustache-desc:
Eustache Deschamps, called Morel for his dark complexion, was a French poet and royal servant of the later fourteenth century. His birthplace was Vertus in Champagne, about 1338 to 1340. He studied under the poet Guillaume de Machaut at Reims and read law at Orléans. He traveled as the king's messenger through Europe, Syria, Palestine, and Egypt, where he is said to have been made a slave for a time. Back in France, Charles V made him a gentleman-usher, and Charles VI kept him on and took him on campaigns in Flanders.

Charles VI later made him governor of Fismes in 1381 and bailiff of Senlis in 1388. He afterward lost the bailiff's post, his pension, and his court office. His ballads, rondels, lays, and virelays are prized less for polish than for the light they throw on the politics and morals of his age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-philli:
George Phillips, a canonist born at Königsberg in 1804, joined the Munich circle that revived Catholic scholarship. Son of an English merchant and a Scotswoman, he studied law at Berlin and Göttingen under Savigny and Eichhorn, taking his doctorate in 1824. Friendship with Jarcke, a Catholic convert, and his own studies of medieval Germany brought Phillips and his wife into the Church in May 1828.

Phillips served Bavaria's Interior Ministry from 1833 and taught history, then law, at Munich from 1834, among Görres, Möhler, Döllinger, and Ringseis. In 1838, with Guido Görres, he founded the militant Historical-Political Papers, still flourishing. Signing a sympathy address in the Lola Montez affair cost him his chair in 1847. He sat for Münster at Frankfurt in 1848, taught at Innsbruck in 1850, and held Vienna's German law chair from 1851 until his death in 1872.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lapland-and-l:
Lapland covers some 150,000 square miles of Europe's far north, from the Atlantic to the White Sea and the Arctic Ocean down to 62 degrees north. Its people, called Lapps by outsiders and Same by themselves, number about 30,000: 2,000 on Russo-Finnish, 8,000 on Swedish, and 20,000 on Norwegian ground.

Midnight sun and months of night, deep forests, bright lakes, cataract rivers, and ice-capped peaks frame their life, with rich iron mines at Gellivare yielding 1,200,000 tons in 1901. Mountain, forest, and fisher Lapps divide the nation, the first two nomadic and living almost wholly by reindeer. Flesh feeds them, milk gives cheese, hides give clothes and tents, and antlers give knife blades and vessels, while winter drives mountain herds down to sheltered valleys.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-desch:
French Jesuit writer Nicolas Deschamps turned his pen against the forces he blamed for corroding faith and social order. Born in 1797, he joined the Jesuits in 1826, taught literature and rhetoric, and wrote on university monopoly, state theology faculties, liberty of association, and communism.

His weightiest book, on secret societies, appeared after his death in 1872 and was revised by Claudio Janet. Tracing Freemasonry back to Manichaeism, Deschamps charged it with working under a cloak of charity against religion, patriotism, and morals alike. Apart from polemics, he wrote didactic and devotional books, including a course of elementary literature.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-philips:
Peter Philips was an English composer of the late Renaissance, born about 1560. Staying loyal to the Church, he left England for the Netherlands and Rome, then returned to Antwerp as organist to Governor Albert's court. In holy orders, he held canonries at Béthune and, from 1612, at Soignies. The title pages of his printed works best trace his wanderings, and their variety shows a life on the move.

He ranks with Tallis, Byrd, Morley, and Gibbons among his age's masters. Canzoni and madrigals for six and eight voices join countless instrumental pieces kept at Antwerp, Leyden, Strasbourg, and London, nineteen of them in the Fitzwilliam Virginal Book. Sacred music drew his best work: motets for five and eight voices, the Gemmulae sacrae, Les rossignols spirituels, and the Deliciae sacrae, with posthumous masses in John IV of Portugal's library.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-victor-august:
Victor Augustin Isidore Dechamps was a Belgian cardinal, Archbishop of Mechlin and Primate of Belgium, who lived from 1810 to 1883. Born at Melle near Ghent, he studied at Tournai and at the Catholic university begun at Mechlin and moved to Louvain, was ordained in 1834. Entered the Redemptorists in 1835, spending four years at Wittem as prefect of students and lecturer in dogmatic theology.

Missionary life began in 1840, with the rectorship at Liège in 1842, a leading part in founding the Confraternity of the Holy Family. He counted his most salutary work, and a share in Liège's historic jubilee of 1845 to 1846. A visit to England showed him the Tractarian movement's effects. As consultor general from 1849 he helped move his congregation's superior general from Pagani to Rome, a transfer completed in 1855.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zips:
Zips is the Hungarian diocese suffragan to Agria, founded by Maria Theresa in 1776 from the exempt provostship of Saint Martin. Its foundation date is unknown but probably early in the thirteenth century. A collegiate chapter also existed at Zips. The provostship stood directly subject to the Holy See, and the provost exercised quasi-episcopal functions. In 1291 Provost Jacobus is mentioned as Bishop of Zips, though the dignity did not pass to his successors.

The chapter originally counted four members. In the thirteenth century Tatars destroyed the church and burnt the archives; after their departure Béla IV had the church rebuilt. Protestantism spread readily in Zips, especially under Stanislav Thurzo, and vigorous Catholic restoration waited until 1641, after which Catholicism progressed better. In 1776 Karl Salbeck became first bishop. The diocese counts 165 parishes, 245 clergy, and 237,140 Catholics.
doe-osti-2584722-how-quantum-sensing-wil: Quantum sensing versus GPS denial got its DOE explainer, and this report covers the warfare application. The pages detail the sensing edge. The defense folks get their briefing. The denial was GPS. The application was warfare. The folks were defense.
doe-osti-3012569-finding-the-missing-pie: Omics gaps got filled, and this DOE text finds the missing model pieces. The pages detail the translation findings. The bio folks get their method. The pieces were missing. The method was bio. The data were omics. The models were translation.
doe-osti-3017514-a-amp-l-annual-report-g: A&L got GRM-MAPS-annualled, and this DOE report covers the year. The pages detail the findings. The researchers get their data. The maps were GRM. The data were researcher. The year was annual. The GRM was MAPS. The A&L was annual.
in-his-steps:
Charles M. Sheldon's In His Steps opens with a minister interrupted at his sermon. The Reverend Henry Maxwell of Raymond is preaching on following in Christ's steps. A shabby young man, out of work, asks him for help and is turned away. The stranger later collapses and dies after challenging the congregation.

Maxwell asks his church members to pledge themselves for one year. Before every act they must ask what Jesus would do, and then do it regardless of cost. A newspaper editor, a singer, a merchant, and a railroad man take the vow. Their businesses, politics, and pleasures change under the test. Sheldon wrote the most influential Christian novel of its age. Its simple question still frames debates about faith, wealth, and duty.
more-hunting-wasps:
J. Henri Fabre's essays on hunting wasps conclude in this volume, translated by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos. The translator's note, dated December 1920, explains the set. Fourteen chapters complete the wasp essays from Fabre's Souvenirs Entomologiques. Companion volumes cover The Hunting Wasps and the Mason-Wasps.

Chapters study the Pompili, the Scoliae, and the Tachytes by name. Others take up a dangerous diet, the Cetonia larva, and changes of diet. Fabre watched wasps paralyze prey and stock their nests with living food for their young. His patient experiments, retold as stories, made him the most beloved insect writer of his age.
observations-upon-the-prophecies-of-dani:
Sir Isaac Newton wrote these studies of Bible prophecy. The book was printed in London in 1733, after his death. It has two parts. One part treats the prophecies of Daniel. The other part treats the Apocalypse of Saint John.

Newton reads prophecy as a guide to past and future history. He works through symbols, kings, and churches in careful order. The dedication addresses Peter, Lord King, the Lord Chancellor. The work shows the famous scientist as a close Bible reader. It remains a key text for his religious thought. Readers still use it to trace his view of history and faith.
on-the-church-steps:
Sarah Hallowell wrote this novel, first printed in parts in 1873. Lippincott's Magazine ran it from August to October. Bessie sits on church steps at the opening. Pine woods and calm lakes lie behind the church. A stiff white pebble walk runs to the gate.

The narrator teases Bessie about bare feet on hard stones. She insists she is not ashamed to sit there. They are good friends, not lovers, she declares firmly. Carriages of local families climb the hill toward them. Social pressure and young love seem set to clash. Hallowell writes a bright, talkative opening scene.
over-the-teacups:
Oliver Wendell Holmes returned to his breakfast-table manner one last time in Over the Teacups, the series of papers begun in March 1888 and finished in his eighties. The preface is dated from Beverly Farm in August 1891. Holmes marvels there at his kind reception. He had felt himself a late comer who had already had his day. He expected the welcome of Monsieur Tonson, the man who comes once too often.

Instead his old readers assured him they were glad to see him. Writing the papers kept him in relation with his fellow beings, he says, and cheated the least promising season of life of its dreariness. He will not promise never to greet his readers again if the impulse proves irresistible. It is the gentlest of literary farewells.
podcast-dannyjones-krJaG5rUPPs:
Ron Miscavige joins Danny Jones for an episode of the KONCRETE Podcast, numbered 74, on the making of his son David Miscavige. David leads the Church of Scientology with an iron hand. Ron was once a church insider and the leader's own father.

Ron tells how David rose from a sickly boy to the head of a global faith. He shares tales of the Sea Org, the church's inner corps, and his own escape by car trunk and road. Jones asks what made his son so hard. Listeners get a father's rare view inside a secret house. The library keeps the talk as an archive record.
podcast-joerogan-mYvGKBCM3Ps:
Oz Pearlman, a well-known mentalist and magician, sits down with Joe Rogan for episode 2332 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Pearlman built his fame by seeming to read minds on stage and on television. Here the act comes into the studio, with Rogan as the willing test subject.

Pearlman performs tricks live and then talks through the craft behind them. He explains how cold reading, sharp observation, and misdirection can make a guess look like mind reading. Rogan pushes him on what is skill and what is showmanship. Listeners get both a magic show and a plain look at how deception really works.
quaint-courtships: Quaint Courtships is a volume of Harper's Novelettes, edited by William Dean Howells and Henry Mills Alden in 1906. Only the contents page is shown here. It lists Margaret Deland's An Encore and Norman Duncan's A Romance of Whooping Harbor. Mary E. Wilkins Freeman's Hyacinthus follows. So do Sewell Ford's Jane's Gray Eyes and Herman Whitaker's A Stiff Condition. May Harris and Francis Willing Wharton also appear. A further piece by Howells closes the list.
richard-hannay-01-the-thirty-nine-steps:
John Buchan's The Thirty-Nine Steps, dated 1915 in its heading, opens the Richard Hannay tales. A letter to Thomas Arthur Nelson explains its making: Buchan, ill one winter, ran out of the shockers he loved and wrote one himself. Chapter one, The Man Who Died, finds Hannay bored in London.

Hannay had made his pile at Bulawayo and come home at thirty-seven, sound and moneyed, yet yawning all day. The evening papers that May day were full of the Near East row and of Karolides, the Greek premier. Hannay calls him the one big man in the show. He vows to give England one more day to fit him to something, or take the next boat for the Cape.
the-altar-steps: The opening pages give the title page and contents of a 1922 New York novel by Compton Mackenzie, printed by George H. Doran Company and called a prelude to The Parson's Progress. Mackenzie, also named as author of Carnival and Poor Relations, dedicates the book to his mother. Chapter heads move from The Bishop's Shadow and The Lima Street Mission to Palm Sunday and life at Nancepean. The last head is The Pomeroy Affair. Church life, family ties, and a wreck are all hinted at along the way.
the-brighton-boys-with-the-flying-corps:
Lieutenant James R. Driscoll wrote The Brighton Boys with the Flying Corps. Its chapters move from a flying squadron and first steps to the front, a fight in the air, and Parker's story. In the Enemy's Country, Planning the Escape, and The Raid on Essen crowd the late heads. The tale opens on a headline in big black type: the war will be won in the air.

Jimmy Hill, a known leader among the boys of the Brighton Academy, reads the paper at the breakfast table. The Academy boys were keen on the war long before the United States joined the Allies. His father, a colonel of French Zouaves, fights on the Western Front. His rare letters home have been passed round the school till the boys know them by heart. Bob Haines' father, too, fanned the war-fire in them.
the-christian-life-its-course-its-hindra: Thomas Arnold, D.D., head master of Rugby School and late Fellow of Oriel College, Oxford, wrote these lectures on the Christian life, taken from the fifth London edition and dated 1856. Only the title page, a long epigraph from Coleridge's Literary Remains, and the start of the contents are present here. The lectures are each built on a Bible text, opening with Genesis on knowing good and evil and Paul's words on putting away childish things. No lecture text follows.
the-story-of-baden-powell-the-wolf-that-: Harold Begbie wrote this illustrated life of Baden-Powell. Its subtitle is The Wolf That Never Sleeps. Grant Richards published it in London in 1900. A reprint followed within the same month of May. Only the title pages are present here, with Begbie's dedication letter. The letter is long and joking. It addresses a Smith Major. Begbie pictures his reader by a sunny river bank. The man sprawls with chin in hands, deep in the book. The biography itself does not appear.
the-thirty-nine-steps:
John Buchan dedicated The Thirty-Nine Steps to his friend Thomas Arthur Nelson in a letter dated September 1915. He calls their shared taste the 'shocker,' the romance where incidents defy probability yet march just inside the possible. Ill in bed one winter, Buchan exhausted his store of such tales and wrote one himself. The contents promise a man who died, a literary innkeeper, a radical candidate, and the Black Stone.

Chapter one finds Richard Hannay back from the City on a May afternoon, disgusted with life after three months in London. That boredom is the spring of the famous spy chase. Buchan's dedication alone tells readers exactly what kind of ride they have bought, and Hannay's ennui makes his plunge into murder and pursuit believable.
till-the-clock-stops:
J. J. Bell, author of Wee MacGreegor, published his novel in 1917 and opens with a prologue in London's City. Inside the Aasvogel Syndicate's directors' room, a young man slowly reads a nineteen-line document on blue handmade paper. A deed done that spring morning will yield complex, extraordinary consequences.

Francis Bullard stands behind him, dark, handsome, and prosperous, toying with a gold nugget on his watch chain. A third, tall and melancholy director warms his palms at the hearth. Readers get a City mystery built from one quiet signing watched by three contrasting men.
trumps: George William Curtis's novel Trumps, dated 1861, survives here through its table of contents. Curtis also wrote Nile Notes of a Howadji and The Potiphar Papers. The chapters open with School Begins and Hope Wayne, then move through society, a New York merchant, and dog-days. A dry-goods firm, Boniface Newt, Son, and Co., gets a chapter of its own. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear.
when-hearts-are-trumps: Tom Hall's verse book When Hearts Are Trumps is shown here by its title pages, a short note, and a contents list, with no poems themselves. Stokes printed the sixth edition in New York in September 1898. Hall thanks the editors of Life, Truth, Town Topics, Vogue, and Munsey's Magazine for leave to reprint. Most of the verses ran in those pages over five years. The contents group poems under Kings and Queens and Bowers. Titles include The Perfect Face, The Kiss, The Bride, and A Rose from Her Hair.
windjammers-and-sea-tramps:
Walter Runciman wrote Windjammers and Sea Tramps, a second edition printed in 1905. He gave the book to John Dent, William Milburn, and the memory of E. H. Watts. Chapter one reaches back to the days of Queen Elizabeth. A Bristol merchant, Thomas Seeley, was jailed in Spain for knocking down a man who slandered the queen.

Elizabeth let her subjects take their own revenge at sea rather than grant his wife's plea for a commission. From that policy, Runciman says, grew the partnership of John Hawkins, Francis Drake, and their queen. Sea power for Britain followed. Runciman, a shipowner, mixes old sea tales with his own years under sail. Salt, trade, and war fill the book.
